sections.title: The main variations
sections.text: In a split squat your feet stay planted in a staggered stance. A reverse lunge steps back on each rep, and a forward or walking lunge steps the body into a new position. A step-up lifts you onto a stable platform, and a rear-foot-elevated split squat makes the exercise harder. The variations overlap, but they differ in balance demand and in how far the knee and hip travel. All of them work well alongside two-legged squats and hinges.

sections.title: Basic technique
sections.text: For a split squat, take a stance wide enough to stand securely, lower straight down by bending the knee and hip under control, then rise through the working leg. Keep your front foot flat on the floor and let the knee follow a comfortable path. A slight forward lean of the torso can be normal. The best stride length depends on your body proportions and what you are training for.

sections.title: Balance and safety
sections.text: While you learn, hold a wall or rail with one hand. If the exercise turns into a balance test, shorten your step, reduce the depth or use less weight until it becomes controlled strength work again. Avoid unstable boxes and very high steps. If the movement keeps causing joint pain, stop or switch to another exercise.

sections.title: Comparing the sides
sections.text: Start with your less confident side, then match its number of good reps on the other side. For example, do two sets of six reverse lunges per leg while holding a support. Small differences between sides don’t mean you are injured, and better control over time is a good goal. Progress by letting go of the support first, then adding reps, then adding resistance.
